question: The Commission is imposing increasingly costly environmental, climate and animal welfare requirements on EU farmers. At the same time, it is steadily opening up the EU market to imports of agricultural products from third countries whose producers are not subject to comparable standards. Successive trade agreements, including with the Mercosur countries and Australia, as well as trade liberalisation with Ukraine are increasing price pressure on European producers. Given the above: 1.
Why is the Commission continuing to conclude and implement agreements that increase imports of cheaper food produced to lower standards, while increasing the operating costs of EU farmers?

Has the Commission carried out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of imports from Ukraine and of agreements with Mercosur, Australia and other partners on the prices, incomes and competitiveness of EU agricultural producers?

Will the Commission support mandatory mirror clauses in all EU trade agreements, or does it intend to continue to tolerate a situation where an EU farmer adheres to strict standards and then has to compete with imports produced without comparable obligations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2026) Trade agreements (FTAs) are carefully designed to open markets for EU exports, diversify supply chains, strengthen partnerships, and improve food-system resilience. The EU agri-food sector is a strong exporter and has benefited from such agreements. EU farmers apply high standards concerning food safety, animal and plant health, animal welfare, and the environment.

All imports placed on the EU market must comply with the relevant EU rules, especially sanitary and phytosanitary requirements – with no exception made to FTA partners. Sensitive sectors are protected via the use of tariff-rate quotas, transition periods, safeguards, or other protections. The Commission regularly carries out impact assessments on trade and agriculture1. It also monitors markets closely.

In the case of Ukraine, it has paid particular attention to impacts on neighbouring Member States and sensitive sectors. As regards the Mercosur and Australia free trade agreements, assessments, stakeholders’ inputs and Member States’ consultations have informed decisions, with special attention to sensitive farm products. The Vision for Agriculture and Food2 focuses on the global level playing field.

The Commission engages globally to promote higher standards, and under the Union domestic framework, the Commission will pursue, in line with international rules, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably on pesticides and animal welfare.
